title: Why Namibia's farming systems developed differently

blocks.heading: Why Namibia's farming systems developed differently
blocks.text: Namibia's farming systems developed through physical and historical conditions. The north receives more rain, so households grow mahangu, sorghum and maize on communal land and keep cattle mainly as wealth and security. The drier centre and south suit extensive cattle, sheep and goat ranching. In the colonial period the centre and south became freehold commercial farms, mostly owned by white settlers, while black farmers were largely confined to communal areas, mainly in the north.

A veterinary cordon fence, the Red Line, separates the north from the centre and south. It protects southern livestock from foot-and-mouth disease and lung sickness, so meat from the south can be exported and large commercial ranches developed there. Northern cattle face quarantine before moving south and restricted access to some export markets, which raises costs and helps keep many northern herds outside commercial production.

blocks.text: After independence in 1990, the Agricultural (Commercial) Land Reform Act of 1995 let the state buy commercial farms offered for sale (“willing buyer, willing seller”) to resettle previously disadvantaged farmers, though progress was slow. The Green Scheme develops irrigation along perennial rivers so that small-scale farmers can grow crops for sale beside commercial operators, for example at Etunda near Ruacana in the Omusati Region, where each irrigates about 3 ha.
Farming systems therefore change. Reliable buyers, water and transport can turn a household's surplus into regular sales, while drought or price falls can push a farm back towards household use.
